Which of the following could be the function that generates the vector field above?
questions.worked_solution:
We notice the following:

- Each vector in our vector field is parallel to the $y$-axis. So, the $i$ and $k$ components of our vector field are zero everywhere. Therefore, we can rule out the following option:

$$
H(x,y,z)=i+k
$$

- Moreover, each vector in our vector field is pointing in the *positive* $y$-direction, so the $j$ component of our vector field is positive. Therefore, we can rule out the following option:

$$
F(x,y,z)=-2\,j
$$

- Finally, we note that each vector in our vector field has the same length, so the $j$ component of our vector field is constant. Therefore, we can rule out the following option:

$$
K(x,y,z)=\operatorname{sin}⁡y\,j
$$

Therefore, we conclude that the diagram corresponds to the vector field $G(x,y,z)=3\,j.$

questions.knowledge_point: Identifying the Local Area Scale Factor of a Transformation
questions.problem:
Consider a small rectangle $Δ$ whose bottom-left corner is located at the point $(1,2)$ with sides parallel to the coordinate axes in the $uv$-plane and whose area is $\delta A.$ Which of the following gives the best approximation for the area of the image of this rectangle under the action of the transformation $T,$ given by

$$
T:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]⟶[\begin{aligned}{u}^{2}+v \\ 2u-{v}^{3}\end{aligned}]?
$$
questions.worked_solution:
Recall that the absolute value of the Jacobian determinant gives the local area scale factor of the transformation at that point:

$$
\text{Area}(T(Δ))≈|\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|\cdot {{\text{Area}(Δ)}_{⏟}}_{\delta A}
$$

 

Computing the corresponding Jacobian determinant, we obtain the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}2u & 1 \\ 2 & -3{v}^{2}\end{aligned}| \\  & =2u\cdot (-3{v}^{2})-1\cdot 2 \\  & =-6u{v}^{2}-2 \\ {\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|}_{(1,2)} & =(-6u{v}^{2}-2)\,{|}_{u=1\,v=2} \\  & =-6(1)(2)^{2}-2 \\  & =-26\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Area}(T(Δ)) & ≈|-26|\cdot \delta A \\  & =26\,\delta A.\end{aligned}
$$

provenance.kp_title: Identifying the Local Area Scale Factor of a Transformation

questions.knowledge_point: Calculating the Displacement of a Particle as a Function of Time
questions.problem: A particle $P$ moves along the $x$-axis in the direction of increasing $x$ where $x\ge 0.$ When the displacement of $P$ from the origin $O$ is $x\,\text{m},$ the magnitude of its acceleration is $8{e}^{1-x}\,{m/s}^{2}$ and is directed toward $O.$ Initially, $P$ is at $x=1\,m$ and has velocity $v=4\,m/s.$ Find $x$ as a function of time $t.$
questions.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14095129/assets/f08c9d1e8dce3c0ae7c37719cadc3fc60bf5de3030ce8c44ca7528a98f3abf7e.png)

Since the acceleration of the particle $P$ has magnitude $8{e}^{1-x}\,{m/s}^{2}$ and is directed *toward* $O,$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=-8{e}^{1-x}.
$$

Using the fact that 

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})
$$

we can rewrite our equation as

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})=-8{e}^{1-x}.
$$

Integrating both sides of the above equation with respect to $x,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})\,\text{d}x & =\int -8{e}^{1-x}\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

which gives the general solution

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =8{e}^{1-x}+K.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $v=4\,m/s$ when $x=1\,m,$ we can find the value of the constant $K,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =8{e}^{1-x}+K \\ \frac{1}{2}(4)^{2} & =8{e}^{0}+K \\ 8 & =8+K \\ K & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =8{e}^{1-x} \\ {v}^{2} & =16{e}^{1-x} \\ v & =\pm 4{e}^{(1-x)/2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Since the particle is moving in the direction of increasing  $x,$ we have that $v(x)>0,$ so we can discard the negative square root. Therefore,

$$
v(x)=4{e}^{(1-x)/2}.
$$

Now, we know that $v=\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}.$ Therefore, we have the equation

$$
\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}=4{e}^{(1-x)/2}.
$$

Separating the variables and integrating both sides with respect to $t,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =4{e}^{(1-x)/2} \\ \frac{1}{{e}^{(1-x)/2}}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =4 \\ \int {e}^{(x-1)/2}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t & =\int 4\,\text{d}t \\ \int {e}^{(x-1)/2}\text{d}x & =\int 4\,\text{d}t \\ 2{e}^{(x-1)/2} & =4t+{C}_{1} \\ {e}^{(x-1)/2} & =2t+C\end{aligned}
$$

where $C=\frac{{C}_{1}}{2}.$ 

We're given that $x=1$ when $t=0.$ Therefore, $C=1,$ and the particular solution is

$$
{e}^{(x-1)/2}=2t+1.
$$

Finally, writing $x$ in terms of $t,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{(x-1)/2} & =2t+1 \\ \frac{x-1}{2} & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(2t+1) \\ x-1 & =2\operatorname{ln}⁡(2t+1) \\ x & =2\operatorname{ln}⁡(2t+1)+1.\end{aligned}
$$

provenance.kp_title: Calculating the Displacement of a Particle as a Function of Time

questions.knowledge_point: Finding a Parametrization of a Surface Defined by an Implicit Cartesian Equation
questions.problem:
$$
r(u,v)=u\,i+v\,j+\text{_____}\,k
$$

The vector-valued function $r(u,v)$ parametrizes the surface defined in Cartesian coordinates as 
$\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+1)-\operatorname{ln}⁡z=\operatorname{ln}⁡2.$
 What is the third component of $r?$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we write the equation of the surface in the form $z=f(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+1)-\operatorname{ln}⁡z & =\operatorname{ln}⁡2 \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡z & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+1)-\operatorname{ln}⁡2 \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡z & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+1}{2}) \\ z & =\frac{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+1}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, a point $(x,y,z)$ on our surface has the corresponding position vector given by

$$
r=x\,i+y\,j+z\,k=x\,i+y\,j+\frac{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+1}{2}\,k.
$$

 

Finally, setting $x=u$ and $y=v,$ we obtain the vector function that parametrizes the surface:

$$
r(u,v)=u\,i+v\,j+\frac{{u}^{2}+{v}^{2}+1}{2}\,k
$$

Therefore, the third component of $r$ is $\frac{{u}^{2}+{v}^{2}+1}{2}.$

provenance.kp_title: Finding a Parametrization of a Surface Defined by an Implicit Cartesian Equation

questions.knowledge_point: Expressing Part of a Sphere in Spherical Coordinates
questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14095129/assets/3358dd177a848ea569fdeab6e39f4be268cc7325bb01c788e9bfe2ea2145d1eb.png)

The solid enclosed by the hemisphere ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}=25$ for $y\ge 0,$ shown above, can be described in spherical polar coordinates as
questions.worked_solution:
We write the position of a point (vector) in spherical polar coordinates as $(\rho ,\theta ,ϕ),$ where 

- $\rho \ge 0$ is the distance from the point to the origin,

- $\theta \in [0,2\pi )$ is the angle between the point and the positive $x$-axis, and

- $ϕ\in [0,\pi ]$ is the angle the corresponding vector makes with the positive $z$-axis.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14095129/assets/e5371e711515feccdaab3f6b10734fb35bb59c724fc408c8b67b4b54132136ec.png)

 

Notice that inside our region, the spherical polar coordinates vary within the following domains:  

- $\rho \in [0,5]$

- $\theta \in [0,\pi ]$

- $ϕ\in [0,\pi ]$

Therefore, we have

$$
{(\rho ,\theta ,ϕ)\,:\,0\le \rho \le 5,\,0\le \theta \le \pi ,\,0\le ϕ\le \pi }.
$$

questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14095129/assets/768046952484d181a404486547db84882424d98da4f677254484e1083580a39b.png)

Which of the following represents the shaded region above as a type II region in two-dimensional space?
questions.worked_solution:
A type II region can be written as

$$
D={(x,y)\,:\,a\le y\le b,\,g(y)\le x\le f(y)},
$$

where $f$ and $g$ are continuous functions.

To express the given region as a type II region, we first rewrite all of the given curves as functions of $y:$

$$
y={x}^{2}\,⟹\,x=\sqrt{y}
$$

The function $x=y$ is already written as a function of $y.$

Notice that the region lies between the horizontal lines $y=0$ and $y=1.$ So, we have $0\le y\le 1.$

We draw a horizontal arrow through the region to determine the left function $g(y)$ and the right function $f(y).$ A horizontal line should intersect the region in a single interval only for it to be a type II region.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14095129/assets/d55cb7ea67d9865368c744577bb4a4b22a3635e8e62869ee65e945612d6c0e98.png)

The horizontal line enters the region through the lower function $x=y$ and leaves through the upper function $x=\sqrt{y}.$ So, we have $y\le x\le \sqrt{y}.$

Therefore, we obtain

$$
D={(x,y)\,:\,0\le y\le 1,\,y\le x\le \sqrt{y}}.
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Finding the Magnitude of a Vector-Valued Function
questions.worked_solution:
Evaluating the function at $t=2,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}r(2) & =⟨\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi (2)}{2}),\,2-1⟩ \\  & =⟨\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi ),\,1⟩ \\  & =⟨0,\,1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the magnitude of this vector, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}|r(2)| & =\sqrt{{0}^{2}+{1}^{2}} \\  & =1\end{aligned}
$$
